summary: Defines a Sieve extension that lets a mail filter push a notification when a message arrives, instead of making users poll for new mail. It leaves the notification method open, expecting things like XMPP or SMS to be used. This is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 8580.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of checking your mailbox again and again, the mailbox can ping you when a letter comes. This lets mail rules send that ping.

subtitle: A Sieve mail-filter action that pushes an instant notification when a message arrives, instead of making users poll.

tldr.problem: Users check for new mail by polling, which is slow for them and costs server resources.
tldr.mechanism: The Sieve extension "enotify" adds a notify action that sends a notification through a method named by a URI, plus tests to check which methods are valid and online, and a modifier to encode URL text.
tldr.outcome: The RFC leaves the notification method open, but requires support for the mailto method so scripts stay portable. It is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 8580.

today: RFC 5435 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8580. It works together with the Sieve base language in RFC 5228.

sections.title: Pushing Notifications from Sieve
sections.content:
Sieve is an email filtering language. RFC 5435 extends it with a new action, notify, for providing instant notifications. The abstract explains the idea: most ways to learn about new mail involve polling, while a push method handled by the final delivery agent gives quicker notifications and saves server resources.

The RFC does not specify notification methods. It expects that existing instant messaging infrastructure such as XMPP, or GSM SMS messages, will be popular. To keep scripts portable, support for the mailto method (RFC 5436) is mandatory. Other methods depend on the implementation and its configuration.

A script enables the extension with the capability string enotify.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail rules can now send you a quick message when something arrives. The notice can go by email, chat or text, and the email kind always works.

sections.title: The notify Action
sections.content:
The usage is notify [":from" string] [":importance" <"1" / "2" / "3">] [":options" string-list] [":message" string] <method: string>. The format of the notification is implementation-defined and depends on the method, but everything given in :message SHOULD be included.

The positional method parameter is a URI, for example a tel URI with a phone number for SMS, or an XMPP URI. Supported values are site-specific. A URI scheme the implementation does not support MUST cause a run-time error, and invalid syntax or an unsupported URI extension MUST cause an error.

The notify action is compatible with all other actions. In particular, it MUST NOT cancel the implicit keep, and several notify actions may run.
sections.plainLanguage: You write a rule that says who to tell, how to tell them, and what to say. The notice does not stop the mail from being filed as usual.

sections.title: Tags: from, importance, options, message
sections.content:
:from names the author of the notification, and its syntax is method-specific. To limit forgery, implementations SHOULD restrict allowed values, and values that fail the restriction are best ignored rather than making the action fail.

:importance is "1" (high), "2" (normal) or "3" (low), with "2" assumed if absent. A method MAY use it as a transport indicator, for example to deliver high importance faster, or to skip low importance notices when the user is marked "busy". If the method has no notion of importance, it MUST be ignored.

:options passes method-specific parameters in the form optionname=value; this RFC defines none. :message is the text to send. The whole string SHOULD be sent, but it MAY be shortened. If absent, an implementation default containing at least the From and Subject header values is RECOMMENDED. Combined with the Sieve variables extension, scripts can build richer messages.
sections.plainLanguage: You can say who the note is from, how urgent it is, and what it says. A one means very urgent and a three means it can wait.

sections.title: Checking Methods and Capabilities
sections.content:
The valid_notify_method test is true only if every listed notification URI is supported and valid, both syntactically and semantically. It performs exactly the same validation as the method parameter of notify, so scripts can avoid run-time errors.

The notify_method_capability test fetches a named capability for a URI and matches it against a key list. It fails (without raising an error) if the URI is invalid or unsupported, or if the capability is unknown. The only capability defined here is online, with values yes, no and maybe. Even "yes" is no guarantee that the notification will arrive.

When both variables and enotify are required, a new set modifier :encodeurl becomes available. It percent-encodes any octet outside the URI unreserved set, which keeps text safe inside a URI. It has precedence 15.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending, a script can ask whether a way of contacting you works and whether you are around right now. Then it picks the best way.

sections.title: Rules for Notification Methods
sections.content:
Documents that define a notification method must follow several rules. Methods MUST NOT add new tags to the notify action. They MAY ignore parameters, and MAY alter the final text, for example by truncating it, if the modifications are documented.

A notification MUST include a way to identify or track its origin, so a recipient can stop the notifications or find out how to contact the sender. Methods MUST say which URI parameters are ignored, used or cause errors, and what the online capability returns.

If sending fails, the interpreter SHOULD ignore the notification and not retry indefinitely. It MAY throttle notifications, and a throttled request MAY be silently ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who invents a new way to send these notes has to follow house rules, such as always saying who sent it and not trying forever if it fails.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC calls notify "potentially very dangerous". The path of a notification may not be secure, an error in the options may send it to the wrong person, and notifications may be forged. Timestamps in particular should not be trusted.

Notifications can cause loops and bounces, and a script notifying several destinations can amplify an attack. So methods MUST provide ways to avoid loops, MUST let administrators limit how many notify actions a script performs (a limit of 1 if there is no use for multiple destinations), and MUST provide logging.

Implementations SHOULD NOT allow variables holding values extracted from the incoming message in the method parameter. Otherwise any sender could make the system an open relay, which in the worst case costs money, for example if the notification is an SMS. Stored scripts must also be protected from unauthorized modification and retrieval.
sections.plainLanguage: A bell that anyone can make ring is a problem. So the rules limit how often it rings, keep a record, and stop strangers choosing who gets the ring.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the Sieve extension enotify and created two new registries. One lists Sieve notification mechanisms, with no initial entries. The other lists notification-capability parameters, with online as the first.

Vendor names start with vnd. and are registered First Come First Served, in the form vnd.<vendor-name>.<mechanism-name>. Others need a Specification Required policy.
sections.plainLanguage: There is an official list of the ways to send notices. Companies can add their own names to it, starting with a special prefix.
